quote: Nominally they are Saivites, but in reality devil-worshippers.
In some parts of the district they speak Telugu and wear the namam (Vaishnavite sect mark) and are apparently immigrants from the Telugu country."
Caste affairs are managed by a Gurikar or headman, and the fines collected are paid to the Sringeri math.
note: Stuart: also 'They are Saivites, and worship Durga and Ganapati'; Karadi Brahmans as purohits. Smarta label inferred from payments to Sringeri; the text does not use the word Smarta.

quote: Chaturakshari.--A sub-division of Satanis, who believe in the efficacy of the four syllables Ra-ma-nu-ja.
note: The syllables are Ra-ma-nu-ja; no Ramanuja tie otherwise stated.

quote: Ekakshara.--A sub-division of Satani.
note: Sect not stated beyond Satani; Om syllable.

quote: Every Dasari is a Tengalai.
note: Stuart: branded 'by the gurus of Tirupati and other shrines'; Francis: 'All Dasaris are Vaishnavites ... branded by some Vaishnavite guru'. Dasaris serve Vaishnava Brahman gurus.

quote: These Dasaris profess the Tengalai form of Vaishnavism, and get themselves branded.
note: Hayavadana Rao.

quote: Dasaris are always Vaishnavites, as the vows are taken only by those castes which are worshippers of that deity.
note: Dedicated to the God at Tirupati by vow.

quote: They are Vaishnavites, and Tulu Brahmans are their priests.
The majority of Devangas are Saivites, and wear the lingam.
note: 'As the Devangas are Lingayats'; Jangams respected. Nandavariki Telugu Brahmans are gurus (see Brahman).

quote: They are Vaishnavites, but some of them also worship Kali or Durga.
note: Priests: Bairagis, occasionally Brahmans.

quote: The Doluvas are Paramarthos, following the Chaitanya form of Vaishnavism, and wearing a rosary of tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) beads.
note: Chaitanya.

quote: The head of the tribe is called the Mutli Guru.
note: Hereditary high priest; 'They profess to be Vaishnavites [and Saivites]'.

quote: the men and women disguise themselves as Dasaris, with perpendicular Vaishnava marks on their foreheads
note: Disguise only; true Dasaris are Vaishnavites branded with Vaishnavite symbols.

quote: The Gamallas are mostly Saivites, and their priests are Aradhya Brahmans, i.e., Telugu Brahmans, who have adopted some of the customs of the Lingayats.
They profess the Vaishnavite religion, and are of the Tengalai persuasion.
note: Brahman gurus reside at Srirangam, Tirupati, and other places; branded with chank and chakram.

quote: In the Madras Census Report, 1891, it is stated that the guru of the Ganigas is the head of the mutt at Sringeri, and that they employ Havig Brahmans for their ceremonies.
note: Thurston adds: 'Sringeri is the name of a Smarta (Saivite) mutt or religious institution at several places, such as Tanjore and Kumbakonam'.

quote: Their guru is the head of the Vyasaraya mutt at Anegundi.
note: Anegundi (Bellary). Madhva label inferred from the Brahman article's list of Madhva mutts (Vayasaraya); Thurston does not say Madhva here.

quote: The Ganigas are both Vaishnavites and Saivites.
note: 'Their guru is known as Dharmasivacharsvami in the Madras Presidency.'

quote: The Onteddu Ganigas are Saivites, and disciples of Lingayat Brahmans (Aradhyas).
note: Some wear sacred thread; some Vaishnava red streak.

quote: Some Gavaras are Vaishnavites, and others Saivites, but difference in religion is no bar to intermarriage.
note: Vaishnavites revere Jagannatha of Puri.

quote: The Sollokhondias are for the most part Paramarthos, i.e., followers of the Chaitanya form of Vaishnavism.
note: Bairagis caste priests.

quote: By religion the Gollas are both Vallamulu (Vaishnavites) and Striramanthulu (Saivites), between whom marriage is permissible.
note: Satanis as priests.

quote: Gudavandlu.--Recorded, in the Nellore Manual, as Vaishnavites, who earn their livelihood by begging.
They are Hindus of the Saivite sect, and wear the sacred thread.
note: Shivalli Brahmans officiate as priests.

quote: They profess the Paramartho or Chaitanya form of Vaishnavism, and also worship Takuranis (village deities).
The Kurukkals are Smartas.
note: Not a Sankaracharya matha statement; sect marks of women same as Nambutiris. This is a Smarta in the sectarian sense.

quote: The Kurukkals are under the spiritual control of certain men in their own caste called Vadhyars.
note: Originally appointed by the Kuppakkara Pottis.

quote: All the Halepaiks of the Kundapur taluk profess to be Vaishnavites, and have become the disciples of a Vaishnava Brahman settled in the village of Sankarappakodlu near Wondse in that taluk.
note: Purified by Vaishnavite mendicant (Dassaya).

quote: As they are disciples of a Lingayat priest at the mutt at Kudli in Mysore, they are Saivites.
note: Fee of eight annas per family at periodical visitations. Thurston calls the priest Lingayat.

quote: The Idaiyans are Vaishnavites, and the more civilised among them are branded like Vaishnava Brahmans.
note: First section Vaishnava (Yadavas); second section demon worshippers/Saiva ash.

quote: They are chiefly Vaishnavites, having Satanis as their priests.
This high-priest, who is called Mahadhipati, is elected by representatives from the chief Jain villages.
note: 'The high-priest has supreme authority over all Jains south of Madras, but not over those in Mysore or South Canara'; Digambara.

quote: The high priest of the Jain basti at Karkal in 1907 gave as his name Lalitha Kirthi Bhattaraka Pattacharya Variya Jiyaswamigalu.
Most of the Vaishnavites are disciples of Bhatrazus.
note: 'There are both Saivites and Vaishnavites among these people, and the former predominate in the southern districts.'

quote: Those among the Saivites who are religiously inclined are disciples of Pandarams of mutts (religious institutions).
strictly speaking, a Jangam is a priest to the religious sect of Lingayats
note: Census 1901: Pattadikaris (head-quarters) and Charamurtis; many are priests to non-Lingayat Sudras.

quote: There is a head mutt (religious institution) at Kadiri, with subordinate mutts at Halori and Bhuvarasu, all in South Canara.
note: Deity Bairava / Gorakshanath; Nath-type cult.
